item.title: Beleaguered at Home, a Bellicose Netanyahu Heads to the U.N.
item.description:
No matter how hostile the reception, for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel, just being able to address the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday as the country’s leader is a personal win in itself.

Against the odds, he has survived politically, even after the policy, military and intelligence debacle that led up to the Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel. His government is about to complete a full, if tumultuous, four-year term, the first Israeli coalition to have done so in more than 30 years.

Yet Mr. Netanyahu will be taking the world stage with his political future on the line, largely directing his words at the audience back home, analysts say, not at the international community from which Israel is more isolated than ever.

A tight race for control of Israel’s Parliament is on the national ballot scheduled for late October. This will be the country’s first election since the day that Hamas led the deadly surprise attack on Israel, igniting the devastating war in Gaza.

As fighting spread to Lebanon, Iran and beyond, the total victory that Mr. Netanyahu promised has remained elusive. Israel’s wars have come to no end. Many Israelis view the coming election as fateful for the future of their deeply shaken and divided country.

Mr. Netanyahu’s conservative Likud party and his far-right and religiously conservative coalition are trailing in the polls. Still, he is Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, a master politician who was made comebacks after being written off, so few are counting him out.

“At one point after Oct. 7, I don’t think anybody anticipated that he would manage to get through a full term.” said Shalom Lipner, who has served as a prime ministerial aide for several Israeli leaders, including Mr. Netanyahu. “But a variety of circumstances aligned to allow him to keep juggling.”

Mr. Lipner, now a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, a centrist research institution, pointed to a combination of Mr. Netanyahu’s political skill, a country distracted and fatigued by three years of war and, he said, “a hapless opposition that was unable to remove him and was outmaneuvered at every turn.”

Mr. Netanyahu’s main rival is Gadi Eisenkot, a centrist former military chief who lost a son and two nephews in the Gaza war and is the front-runner in a political bloc unified primarily in its opposition to Mr. Netanyahu and his coalition.

Mr. Eisenkot has been beating Mr. Netanyahu in surveys asking about suitability for the top office. But currently the polls show that the opposition would need the support of at least one of the predominantly Arab parties to form a government. It could either include them in a majority coalition or exclude them from the government but gain their backing to assemble a fragile minority coalition.

Any reliance on Arab parties is a prospect that many Jewish voters reject, and that Mr. Netanyahu has been inciting against, even though Israel’s foundational Declaration of Independence promised “complete equality of social and political rights” to all the country’s citizens.

The final outcome may be determined by the fate of a few small parties that may or may not scrape past the electoral threshold for representation in Parliament. They could tip the calculations for the inevitable post-election coalition math.

Mr. Netanyahu has become an increasingly polarizing figure in the aftermath of the Oct. 7 attack, having refused to take any personal responsibility for the failure that led to the deadliest day in Israel’s history. He has also failed to establish an independent commission of inquiry.

That attack killed about 1,200 people in Israel, most of them civilians, and took some 250 others hostage, according to the Israeli authorities. More than 70,000 Palestinians were killed in the ensuing war, including thousands of children, according to the Gaza health ministry, which does not distinguish between combatants and civilians. Much of Gaza had been left in ruins, many of its people displaced and destitute, and human rights groups and foreign governments have accused Israel of war crimes.

A more combative Israel, along with rampant settlement expansion and violence in the occupied West Bank, have left the country increasingly isolated internationally. Old friends in Washington have warned of eroding support for Israel across the board in the United States, Israel’s most critical ally.

Even before Oct. 7, Israel was in turmoil over a divisive government plan to overhaul the judiciary in a way that opponents called antidemocratic. The plan was put forward as Mr. Netanyahu stands trial on corruption charges.

“This election is about what kind of Israel there will be here,” said Gayil Talshir, a political scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. “Will it be a nationalist, racist, antidemocratic, illiberal state and an international pariah? Or one that repairs the democratic rules of the game, invests in high tech, education and welfare.”

The old Israeli doctrine of waging short wars that end with security or diplomatic agreements has gone. “Netanyahu is leading Israel to a war with no victory and stretching the military to its limits,” she said.

Mr. Netanyahu has neglected Israel’s international standing out of narrow interest, Ms. Talshir said, prioritizing the demands of his extremist coalition partners to stay in power.

Former aides to Mr. Netanyahu say his mission to maintain his grip on power is driven by a belief that nobody else is capable of taking on the challenges Israel faces.

Mr. Netanyahu plans to make a lightning one-day visit to New York to deliver his speech at the annual U.N. General Assembly. He is likely to speak to a near-empty hall. Last year, as he approached the podium, dozens of international delegates staged a walkout in protest over Israeli actions in Gaza.

But Mr. Netanyahu, rarely put off, will relish the opportunity to present himself as Israel’s leading statesman, analysts said.

He appeared to be arriving in a bellicose mood. This week his office shared a government-produced video depicting the General Assembly as an anti-Israel echo chamber filled with parrots squawking, “Blame Israel.”

Mr. Netanyahu is likely to speak about Israel’s military achievements in degrading the capabilities of its enemies, analysts said, and he may threaten them with future action.

Mr. Netanyahu’s office said on Thursday that he would be meeting in New York with several foreign leaders, including from Argentina, Ethiopia, Greece and Papua New Guinea. “Many world leaders requested to meet with the prime minister during the visit,” his office said in a statement, adding that because of a tight schedule and the need to return to Israel in time for the onset of a Jewish holiday, “he was only able to accommodate some of them.”

No meeting has been arranged with President Trump, who has so far refrained from openly endorsing Mr. Netanyahu’s candidacy. While Mr. Netanyahu had long championed his close working relations and friendship with Mr. Trump as a winning ace, the relationship has become complicated in recent months as Israeli and American interests diverge over Iran.

But Mr. Netanyahu always has the option of reverting to his previous tactic, used under Democratic administrations, of presenting himself as the only Israeli politician who can stand up to an American president.

Given the polls, analysts say, his best hope may be an inconclusive election result in which neither side secures a solid majority in Parliament. “The most likely outcome is that Netanyahu loses but the opposition doesn’t win,” Mr. Lipner, the former aide, said.

Referring to the small parties that may not cross the electoral threshold, meaning that their votes will go to waste, Mr. Lipner said, “We are all talking about the big issues, but it’s the technical minutiae that may determine where we end up.”

item.title: As Russia Steps Up Shadow War, Europeans Waver on How to Respond
item.description:
An explosive-laden drone at a German airport. A strike on a passenger train near the Polish border. A rush of warnings about more chaos to come.

If President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia was hoping to heap pressure on Ukraine’s closest allies, he’s succeeded with a series of provocations that Western officials have blamed on Russia and said could put citizens of NATO countries in danger.

The question is how Europe responds.

In the past week, European leaders have spoken with uncommon urgency about Russia’s shadow war. Prime Minister Donald Tusk of Poland, citing unspecified intelligence, said Moscow may be planning attacks in Europe. “No one is safe,” President Emmanuel Macron of France cautioned. The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, told the U.N. General Assembly that his country faced an “industrial-scale assault” in terms of information warfare.

Their theory is that Mr. Putin, bogged down on the battlefield, is stepping up attacks on Ukraine’s supporters, hoping to sow fear and panic and, ultimately, weaken their support for Kyiv.

It won’t work, says the NATO secretary, Mark Rutte. “Russia wants us to stop helping Ukraine,” he said in a recent address. “Their actions will only lead us to do more for Ukraine.”

For years, officials and experts have accused Mr. Putin of targeting Europe with hybrid attacks — hostile actions that are designed to evade culpability, and that generally stop just short of inflicting enough damage to trigger a forceful response. What has changed, according to Charlie Edwards, a former British intelligence official now at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, is the “potential lethality and operational ambition of Russian sabotage operations.”

German investigators this month concluded that Russian operatives sent a drone equipped with military-grade explosives to Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany over the summer. Had the drone exploded, officials said, it would have caused significant damage and possibly killed people.

Earlier this month, a Russian drone smashed into a passenger train in western Ukraine, perilously close to the Polish border, as foreign visitors were leaving a diplomatic conference in Kyiv. It was widely seen as a warning to Ukraine’s allies.

“We have to be prepared more, and we have to understand that this activity is now becoming almost ever-present,” the European Union’s top military adviser, Gen. Sean Clancy of Ireland, said in an interview.

On Wednesday, President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine warned that Russia’s war would continue to spread unless allies responded. “The more freedom Putin has to act, the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else,” he said in a speech in New York.

The Kremlin has consistently denied involvement in hybrid activities. Russia’s foreign minister, Sergey V. Lavrov, has pointed instead to what he calls Western “large-scale political, economic, and coercive measures, including sanctions.”

“This is the hybrid war,” he said in a recent speech.

Western security officials say they have seen no sign of Russia preparing for a conventional war with NATO. Rather, officials say, Mr. Putin and his overstretched forces are looking for ways to undermine Kyiv and its allies.

“Russia doesn’t have the capacity to challenge NATO” right now, Baiba Braze, the minister of foreign affairs for Latvia, said in an interview in Riga.

“They cannot move the front,” she said. “They are not gaining territory.”

What Moscow can do, though, is continue to pursue relatively low-cost hybrid attacks.

That has included sending drones into NATO territory to surveil military bases and disrupt commercial air traffic, jamming navigation systems of passenger planes, and hacking into energy grids and dams. Last week alone, a Russian warship fired flares at a Danish helicopter over international waters, and a NATO fighter jet shot down a drone that had likely entered Lithuanian airspace from Belarus, a Russian ally.

“An attack will occur at the point when political intent, military readiness, and strategically favorable timing come together to allow it to happen,” Germany’s deputy defense minister, Nils Schmid, said last week.

“Our task — Europe’s task — is to make such a perceived favorable timing permanently impossible for Moscow,” he said.A challenge for Europe is that the United States seems less inclined to take a hard line on Russia. The Trump administration has even invited Mr. Putin to attend a Group of 20 summit in Miami in December.

European nations have spent the years since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine trying to stop Russia by issuing economic sanctions, freezing financial assets, expelling diplomats and naming-and-shaming Moscow for attacks. Yet Russia appears undaunted.

“The discussion has been if deterrence works when it comes to hybrid operations, and I would say, not well enough,” the Swedish defense minister, Pal Jonson, said in a recent interview.

The top E.U. diplomat, Kaja Kallas, is urging leaders to more aggressively pursue those penalties and, potentially, reduce the number of Russian tourists allowed into European nations. She also called last week for bolstering protections against Russian disinformation and recruitment.

Some security experts are pushing NATO to consider creating a new level of alliance-wide response to hybrid attacks. But the idea is in its early stages and remains theoretical for now.

Many European officials argue that continuing to send military support to Ukraine is the best way to keep Russia at bay. Just days after the train strike near its border, Poland pledged to send Ukraine additional Patriot interceptors — they are in scarce supply worldwide — to help defend against Russian ballistic missiles.

“This is the message: Regardless of your actions, Russia, we will support Ukraine even more,” Lt. Gen. Krzysztof Krol, assistant to the chief of staff of Poland’s armed forces, said in an interview.

Moscow is changing its tactics, he said, “sharpening their activities” to keep Europe off-balance.

After days of urgent warnings, European officials now seem eager to project steadiness.

“Russia is facing big difficulties when it comes to Ukraine, big difficulties, and we have to stay calm,” Mr. Rutte said Wednesday. “We also have to carry on.”

Mr. Macron said Europe must resist the urge to overreact. “Deterrence should remain discreet,” he said. “We must not show our hands.”

Adam Goldman contributed reporting from Riga, Latvia, and Michael Schwirtz from London.

item.title: Scandal Comes for the Judge Who Jailed Brazil’s Former President
item.description:
He cracked down on a deluge of online lies. He punished rioters falsely claiming a stolen election. And he jailed a former president who tried to stage a coup.

Depending on whom you ask, this made Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes either a hero who protected Brazil’s democracy or a villain deploying authoritarian means to target the far right.

His decisions have turned him into a polarizing figure in the complicated global debate over the limits and policing of what can be said online — and drew the ire, and sanctions, of President Trump.

Now, an explosive scandal linking Justice Moraes to a disgraced banker at the center of a multibillion dollar fraud scheme has plunged Brazil’s highest court into a crisis, reshaping a narrow presidential election just weeks away.

The crisis began when another justice made public a damning police dossier suggesting that Justice Moraes may have exchanged dozens of messages with the banker, Daniel Vorcaro.

In texts apparently sent to Justice Moraes, Mr. Vorcaro asked for help avoiding arrest. In other exchanges with associates, Mr. Vorcaro mentioned paying millions to a law firm run by the justice’s wife.

The police have not determined what Justice Moraes texted back or whether he aided Mr. Vorcaro in any way. But, overnight, the revelation has become a major electoral issue, outraging Brazilians and setting off calls to hold Justice Moraes and the Supreme Court accountable.

The scandal has also energized the Brazilian right, rallying support for the right-wing presidential candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, because Justice Moraes jailed his father, Jair Bolsonaro, on charges of trying to retain power after losing the last election.

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a leftist, has been saddled with the fallout of an institutional crisis unfolding on his watch and blemishing the reputation of Justice Moraes, an important ally.

Flávio Bolsonaro, who is challenging Mr. Lula in next month’s vote, has rushed to link his rival to the justice at the center of the scandal. “To vote for Lula is to vote for Alexandre de Moraes,” Mr. Bolsonaro recently told a crowd of supporters.

“It gave Flávio’s campaign a simple slogan,” said Luciano da Ros, a Brazilian political scientist. “And it united different segments on the right around a powerful common enemy.”

The crisis engulfing the judiciary has provided another advantageous twist for Mr. Bolsonaro. It has eclipsed revelations that he himself is being investigated by the authorities for raising millions of dollars from Mr. Vorcaro to finance a biopic about his father.

Mr. Lula, eager to shield his campaign, has tried to distance himself from Justice Moraes. “Nobody is above the law,” he said in an interview, urging an investigation into the justice’s conduct.

Though he did not appoint Justice Moraes to the Supreme Court, Mr. Lula has lauded his tough stance aimed at protecting Brazil’s institutions. “I can assure you that Alexandre de Moraes is a serious person,” he told The New York Times last year. “I place full trust in the judiciary to do its job.”

During the last presidential election, Mr. Lula faced off against Mr. Bolsonaro’s father in a major test for the nation’s democracy. The judiciary, led by Justice Moraes, played a key role in defending the vote’s integrity and ensuring a peaceful transfer of power.

Now, ahead of another showdown between Mr. Lula and a Bolsonaro, the court may again be called on to play a defining role in an election, which could gauge whether the left can stop the right’s momentum in capturing presidencies in multiple Latin American countries.

“The court has revealed itself to be fragile,” said Thiago Amparo, a professor of law and human rights at the Getúlio Vargas Foundation, a Brazilian research institute. “And that makes it vulnerable to new challenges that may arise.”

Justice Moraes, who did not respond to a list of questions for this article, has not yet explained his relationship with Mr. Vorcaro.

Without offering evidence, he has suggested the documents implicating him may be the handiwork of foreign actors looking to meddle in the elections. And he has accused a colleague, appointed by the older Mr. Bolsonaro, of trying to sway the vote.

That justice, André Mendonça, has come under fire for sidestepping protocol to release the dossier implicating Justice Moraes, even as he kept secret for months a police investigation into Flávio Bolsonaro for potential corruption and money laundering.

Justice Mendonça, who did not reply to a request for comment, has rejected accusations of political bias in his handling of a sprawling fraud investigation involving Mr. Vorcaro that has ensnared a vast swath of Brazil’s elite.

As part of this investigation, the police seized Mr. Vorcaro’s cellphone and recovered over 50 messages suggesting he may have sought assistance from Justice Moraes to avoid investigation and, later, arrest.

Mr. Vorcaro also made reference in the dossier to payments made to a law firm partially owned by the justice’s wife, which he had hired to consult his bank in a contract worth more than $25 million. Digital data shows that Justice Moraes had edited that contract, according to the police.

Justice Moraes has drawn right-wing wrath by aggressively investigating, prosecuting and censoring anyone the court deemed a threat to Brazil’s democracy. Mr. Bolsonaro’s movement has been the prime target.

When Jair Bolsonaro and his allies attacked the integrity of Brazil’s voting machines, Justice Moraes ordered social media platforms to take down thousands of posts and accounts spreading baseless claims of fraud.

When Mr. Bolsonaro’s supporters stormed government buildings in January 2023, upset that he had lost and echoing his claims of a stolen election, Justice Moraes ordered the arrest of state security officials and sentenced rioters to years in prison.

And when the court’s investigation found Mr. Bolsonaro and his inner circle had planned a coup and plotted to assassinate Mr. Lula and Justice Moraes, the justice oversaw the trial, conviction and sentencing of the former president to 27 years in prison.

“With all the errors and successes typical of an institution made up of human beings, the Supreme Court has been, and will continue to be, a barrier against attempts to undermine the democratic rule of law,” Justice Moraes said at an event in 2023.

Yet in his quest to protect democracy, Justice Moraes has also jailed people without trial and censored online speech, with little transparency or room for appeal.

Justice Moraes and his defenders have claimed his actions were necessary in the face of an extraordinary threat to Brazil’s democracy. Others have argued his heavy-handed tactics represent their own antidemocratic threat.

Last year, that debate reached Washington: in an effort to help Mr. Bolsonaro avoid prison, President Trump targeted Justice Moraes with harsh sanctions. They were later lifted, though Mr. Bolsonaro’s allies are lobbying Washington to reinstate them.

In Brazil, the revelations linking Justice Moraes to the banker have prompted calls for an investigation and even impeachment. And, among many Brazilians, they have raised questions about the health of a vital institution.

Supreme Court justices are nominated by Brazil’s president and approved by the Senate. While presidential appointments can influence the court’s ideological leaning, justices are meant to remain independent from other branches of government.

But, increasingly, the court has been seen as taking political sides.

For one, the court played a key role in Mr. Lula’s political comeback when it tossed out corruption convictions barring him from holding office, paving the way for his victory over Mr. Bolsonaro in 2022.

And when the court convicted Mr. Bolsonaro, it effectively made the nation’s most popular right-wing leader ineligible to run for office ever again.

Now the court itself has landed at the center of a political firestorm.

Under pressure, the court’s chief justice swiftly curbed the vast judicial powers that Justice Moraes employed for years to wage war on internet falsehoods. The court also held a dramatic session that transfixed the nation last week to decide whether to investigate Justice Moraes, an unprecedented move for the judiciary.

After hours of heated debate and finger-pointing, allies of Justice Moraes postponed the decision until after the elections.

Since then, new revelations have linked Mr. Vorcaro to other Supreme Court justices, including the justice now overseeing the nation’s electoral authority, deepening the crisis.

With Justice Moraes sidelined and public trust in tatters, experts worry the court may struggle to rebuff new attacks on Brazil’s institutions such as electoral meddling by the United States, A.I.-powered disinformation, or a contested vote if Mr. Bolsonaro loses.

Other, less assertive justices now at the helm are unlikely to be as “swift and decisive” as Justice Moraes, Mr. Ros said.

“This represents a fall from grace,” he added. “And that means every decision they make is more likely to be questioned.”

Thayz Guimarães and Alice Maciel contributed reporting from Brasília.

item.title: Son of Israeli Ambassador to U.S. Critically Hurt in West Bank Attack, Officials Say
item.description:
The son of Israel’s ambassador to the United States was critically injured after a Palestinian man rammed his car into a military checkpoint in the West Bank, the Israeli authorities have said.

Violence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank has surged in recent weeks, fueling growing worries that the territory could erupt.

The injured man, Neria Leiter, 39, a reserve soldier and the son of Ambassador Yechiel Leiter, was hurt after a Palestinian man drove into a security checkpoint northwest of Jerusalem on Wednesday, the Israeli military said in a statement. The military added that the assailant had been shot dead.

The Palestinian authorities said that Mahmoud Suleiman, 29, a Palestinian man, had been killed by Israel forces in that area but did not say whether he had attacked the checkpoint.

Mr. Leiter said in a video statement on Thursday from Shaare Zedek Medical Center in Jerusalem, the hospital where his son was being treated, that his son’s life was “hanging in the balance.”

The latest attack occurred as violence in the West Bank has soared in the wake of the Israeli war in Gaza that followed the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.

On Sunday, the eve of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, a Palestinian man shot and killed an Israeli man in the West Bank, according to the Israeli authorities, who said that they had detained a suspect over the shooting.

That attack came as Israeli settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank has hit record levels, according to U.N. data, with the Israeli authorities appearing to do little to stop them in some cases. In 2026, at least 18 Palestinians have been killed in clashes with settlers, the U.N. humanitarian office reported.

The Israeli military has also started sweeping raids in the territory, saying that troops are targeting Palestinian armed groups.

Israeli forces have killed more than 1,000 Palestinians in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, including about 80 this year, according to the U.N. humanitarian office.

Several former Israeli generals have condemned the rise in settler attacks as “Jewish terrorism” and criticized the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for not doing enough to stop them. In March, Israel’s top general for the West Bank, Maj. Gen. Avi Bluth, said in an open letter that violence by Israeli civilians against Palestinians could set the territory ablaze.

Mike Huckabee, the U.S. ambassador to Israel, has condemned the increased targeting of Palestinians in the West Bank as “terrorist” attacks.

Palestinian armed groups have also carried out deadly attacks against Israeli civilians in the territory. More than 40 Israelis have been killed in the West Bank over the past three years, according to the U.N. data.

Mr. Leiter’s older son, Moshe Leiter, a reservist in an elite naval unit, was killed during the first months of the Israeli war in Gaza.

Alexander Ioscovich, deputy director general of Shaare Zedek Medical Center, said in a statement that Neria Leiter was in “stable” condition but that his life remained at risk.

Mr. Netanyahu visited the hospital shortly before departing for the United Nations General Assembly in New York, his office said in a statement.

Adam Rasgon, Gabby Sobelman, Fatima AbdulKarim and Aaron Boxerman contributed reporting.

item.title: Party Close to King Leads in Morocco’s Election as Young Voters Stay Away
item.description:
Early results from legislative elections in Morocco put a party close to the country’s monarchy in the lead on Thursday. But voter turnout was the lowest in nearly two decades as disillusioned young people stayed away from the polls.

The elections, held on Wednesday, were the first since two major crises in Morocco: anti-government Gen Z protests in 2025 and the deadly mass crossing of migrants into Ceuta, an entry point to the European Union on the country’s northern coast, this summer.

Twenty-seven parties were competing for 395 seats in the lower house of Parliament, and preliminary results showed that the political status quo appeared to be largely intact. The top three parties, according to the results, are part of the coalition that has governed Morocco since 2021.

Morocco is a constitutional monarchy, and the king will appoint a prime minister from the party with the most seats. Because no single party won an outright majority, parties will now work to form a coalition.

The election was dominated by frustration with unemployment and poor public services, as well as concern over people leaving Morocco in search of better economic opportunities. Voter turnout was the lowest since 2007, at 38 percent, according to figures released by the interior ministry.

The Authenticity and Modernity Party, a centrist party, took an early lead by winning 97 seats. Part of the current governing coalition, it was founded by a childhood friend and close adviser to the king.

One of the most likely contenders for prime minister is Fouzi Lekjaa, a member of that party who is currently budget minister and the president of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation. King Mohammed IV is betting that Morocco’s co-hosting of the 2030 soccer World Cup will boost the country’s economy and image.

The National Rally of Independents, a member of the governing coalition and the party of the outgoing prime minister, secured 66 seats, suffering losses. A third coalition party, the Independence Party, won 65 seats, while the Justice and Development Party, an Islamist party that lost power in 2021, increased its share of seats from 13 to 54.

The interior ministry said voting had proceeded normally, apart from isolated incidents. But the Left Alliance, a small left-wing party, and the Moroccan Association for Human Rights said they had documented irregularities at several polling stations. Prosecutors said on Wednesday that they had opened two investigations in Tangier, one involving a man who was detained with a bag containing ballots at a school being used as a polling center.

Young voters in Morocco appeared especially disenchanted by the election. People aged 18 to 24 make up 12 percent of the population but just 4 percent of the country’s 15.8 million registered voters.

“For me, it is difficult to believe that these elections can bring meaningful institutional change,” said Ayoub Boudad, a 31-year-old filmmaker who did not vote. “When major priorities seem to be decided far away from elected institutions, elections can lose their meaning in the eyes of a generation.”

Morocco’s economy grew by a fairly robust 4.9 percent last year, driven in part by World Cup spending, according to figures from the World Bank. But unemployment is high — 13 percent last year — and about one-third of young Moroccans are jobless.

In 2025, frustrations spilled out into widespread Gen Z protests that were met with a police crackdown. Then, this summer, more than 70,000 migrants rushed into Ceuta, a tiny Spanish exclave squeezed between Morocco and the Mediterranean, seeking jobs and better lives.

Young people have also expressed dissatisfaction with their leaders’ willingness to normalize relations with Israel. Under the outgoing government, Morocco and Israel agreed to open embassies in their respective countries — a move that many Moroccans saw as an affront to their solidarity with Palestinians.

item.title: Forced Eviction of 87-Year-Old Woman Spurs Outrage in Spain
item.description:
Demonstrations that erupted after the police broke down an 87-year-old woman’s door to evict her from the Madrid apartment where she had lived most of her life brought Spain’s housing and affordability crisis to the front burner of the country’s politics on Thursday.

Thousands of protesters took to the streets across the country on Wednesday amid an outcry over the eviction of María del Carmen Abascal, who was brought out of her apartment on a stretcher from apparent exhaustion and was still in the hospital as of Thursday afternoon.

The eviction has touched a nerve among Spaniards angry over rising housing prices, and it has heaped pressure on the leader of Spain’s left-wing government, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who last year promised that housing would be his government’s priority.

Ms. Abascal’s eviction sparked a new round of political finger-pointing, with progressive politicians blaming conservatives, while conservatives played the case down and accused opponents of rabble-rousing.

The eviction came as Mr. Sánchez spoke at the United Nations General Assembly, seeking to present himself and Spain as an alternative to authoritarian politics and as a standard-bearer of humane liberalism. In a speech on Wednesday morning, alongside Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York, Mr. Sánchez touted his government’s social policies, including restrictions on evictions.

The uproar over the eviction followed Mr. Sánchez to New York, where the first question he faced at a news conference on Wednesday afternoon was about Ms. Abascal’s situation. His government, he said, would provide a “response” to what he called a “social tragedy."

As the eviction was being carried out, hundreds of activists had barricaded themselves outside the home of Ms. Abascal, known as “Maricarmen,” in an ultimately unsuccessful attempt to prevent it.

“Where is the progressive government?” protesters chanted outside Ms. Abascal’s home.

“I really don’t understand how it is possible that the government can’t do anything,” Ms. Abascal’s lawyer, Beatriz Duro, said in an interview. “She is an older woman; she is a woman whose physical decline we have seen in real time, someone who has lived and suffered.”

Ms. Duro declined a request for an interview with her client, saying that Ms. Abascal was still convalescing in a hospital and overwhelmed by the media attention.

Ms. Duro said the national government had tried to reach an agreement with Urbagestión, the real estate company that owns the apartment, but that the effort had failed. Urbagestión did not respond to a request for comment on Thursday.

Ms. Abascal’s father had held the lease for the apartment when the family moved there in the 1950s. He passed it on to his wife, who in turn passed the rent-controlled apartment to Ms. Abascal in 2005.

In 2020, the property was bought by Urbagestión, which raised her rent from €500 ($570) to €2,650 a month, far more than she could afford on her monthly pension of €1,350, Ms. Duro said.

The company tried to evict her three times, but courts blocked the attempts until the case reached Spain’s Supreme Court, which ruled in favor of the owner, arguing that her inherited rent-controlled lease had legally expired under Spanish law.

Mr. Sánchez’s minority government could send a bill to Parliament as early as next week that would make evictions more difficult, but it is unclear whether it would pass. A party on which Mr. Sánchez has repeatedly depended to pass legislation is more supportive of landlords’ rights. A similar bill failed to pass in February.

If that legislation had passed, Mr. Sánchez said on Wednesday, “we would not have the situation that Maricarmen is experiencing.” He blamed a political opponent, the conservative regional leader of Madrid, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, for letting the eviction happen.

Ms. Ayuso played down the significance of the case on Thursday, calling it “one eviction out of the 25,500 that take place every year in Spain.” She also accused Mr. Sánchez of encouraging people to protest.

Right-wing parties across Spain argue that progressive housing policies that expand tenants’ rights hurt small property owners and encourage squatting. In 2025, Ms. Ayuso called Mr. Sánchez an “accomplice” of squatters.

Ms. Abascal, caught in the middle of the political furor, may go to live with a relative in a one-bedroom apartment in another province, “but that’s not a solution,” Ms. Duro said.

item.title: Saudi Arabia Downs Houthi Missiles Targeting Kingdom, Official Says
item.description:
The Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen said on Thursday that it had shot down six ballistic missiles fired by the Iran-backed Houthi militia, in what appeared to be one of the largest cross-border attacks by the group since its conflict with Saudi Arabia spiraled back into war.

The missiles were aimed at the Saudi cities of Taif and Yanbu, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, a spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, said on social media. “Escalations and violations by the terrorist Houthi militia will be dealt with firmly,” he added, without specifying where the missiles were intercepted.

The Saudi authorities issued alerts on Thursday warning of potential attacks in cities across Saudi Arabia, including Mecca, home to the holiest sites in Islam, before announcing that the danger had passed.

The Houthis did not immediately comment on the Saudi claims.

The Houthis’ ability to target Taif and Yanbu, cities that are far from the Yemeni border with Saudi Arabia, underscores how the militia’s arsenal and its ambitions have grown since the war between the two sides flared up in recent weeks.

The barrage of missiles was launched a day after Saudi Arabia began celebrations for its National Day, a holiday marked by public gatherings and events across the country.

For more than a decade, Yemen’s civil war has pitted the Houthis, a Shiite Muslim group that casts itself as an anti-imperialist movement trying to liberate the country, against the internationally recognized government backed by Saudi Arabia. A fragile truce was agreed in 2022 and the fighting had mostly abated. But the conflict reignited this year in the wake of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, adding to broader Middle East tensions that have disrupted the global economy.

item.title: Stabbing in Poland Leaves Priest Dead and Adds to Tension With Ukraine
item.description:
The police in southeastern Poland arrested a citizen of Ukraine on suspicion of carrying out a knife attack on Thursday that, according to state-owned news media, killed a priest and wounded four others at a Roman Catholic abbey near the border with Ukraine.

Officials in the Subcarpathia region of Poland said in a statement that the Ukrainian, 31, who was not named, attacked four men and a woman Thursday morning at the abbey, a 17th-century Benedictine nunnery in the town of Jaroslaw.

TVP Rzeszow, the local branch of the state broadcasting network, reported that the priest, one of three clergy members wounded, had died.

The motive for the attack was not immediately clear. Ukrainian nationals living in Europe, particularly young, jobless men fleeing the war against Russia, have been a frequent target for recruitment by Russian agencies looking for operatives to carry out sabotage and other attacks in Poland and elsewhere.

Some Ukrainians living in Poland, however, faced with what they see as rising antagonism against their presence, have expressed hostility against their host country of their own accord.

The knife attack on Thursday followed a series of small but sometimes violent street scuffles between Poles and Ukrainian refugees, millions of whom fled into Poland after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Many have since returned home or moved on to other European countries, but the Polish Interior Ministry in August estimated that at least 1.8 million remained in Poland.

Far-right Polish politicians have sought to stoke the animosity, accusing Ukrainian refugees of abusing Poland’s hospitality, which includes access to schools and free health care. Poland has stopped providing free housing and rolled back some of its support for Ukrainian refugees but has made no move to send them home.

The far right in Poland often plays on bitter memories dating to World War II, when Ukrainian nationalists massacred tens of thousands of Poles in a western region of Ukraine that was then part of Poland.

In May, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, added to the tensions by signing a decree honoring wartime nationalist fighters whom Poles hold responsible for those killings, which the Poles call the Volhynia Genocide.

Poland’s government, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, a centrist, has worked to restore relations to an even keel, alarmed that a rupture over history would imperil one of the closest alliances in Eastern Europe against Russia.

Much of the American and European weaponry and ammunition provided to Ukraine passes through bases and travels on highways and railroads through Poland.

Anatol Magdziarz contributed reporting.
